Claude Code 2.1.310 · Opus 5.5 · seed 1 · 21 + 61 runs

Does scattering of the change relate to the agent’s effort, navigation and success?

Question. When the agent’s change is spread over more files, packages and loosely connected code, does it spend more tool calls, cost and searches, and does it still pass? Scattering is measured on the agent’s own final diff, not on the reference patch, since a reference commit can contain unrelated changes.

What “effort” means here. The measures of how much work the agent did in a run:
MeasureWhat it counts
Tool callsevery action: a shell command, a file read, an edit, a test run
API turnshow many times the model was called (one turn = the model thinks and replies once, usually with a tool call)
Cost (USD)the run’s cost as reported by Claude Code: output, new input, cache writes and re-read context
Searchessearch commands: grep, rg, find, git grep, and the Grep/Glob tools
Wall timeseconds from start to finish
The appendix’s benchmark comparison adds output tokens, re-read context tokens, test runs, probe scripts and re-edits.
These are mostly one thing measured several ways. Tool calls and API turns are almost identical (ρ ≈ 1.0 in both benchmarks); cost tracks them at ≈ .9 on FeatureBench and ≈ .8 on SWE-Pro. Read “scattering relates to tool calls, turns and cost” as one finding. On FeatureBench searches also move with tool calls (ρ .96), so they add little separate evidence there; on SWE-Pro they are more distinct (ρ .74).

Key findings

Only results that hold after correcting for multiple tests. SWE-Pro (61 runs): raw links between scattering and effort survive correction; none survive after the size adjustment.

Do scattered changes cost the agent more?
Yes, beyond their size.

  • Runs whose change spans more files or packages use more tool calls, cost and searches, even after adjusting for size (FeatureBench ρ ≈ +0.5 to +0.65, surviving correction).
  • SWE-Pro (61 runs): the same direction before the size adjustment (ρ ≈ +0.3 to +0.5, surviving correction), but not after it (ρ ≈ +0.1 to +0.35, q ≥ .11). On SWE-Pro, scattering mostly tracks size. Adding 11 multi-file tasks (batch 4) did not change this.
  • Focus: when most of the change sits in one file, the run is cheaper (ρ ≈ −0.55).
  • Functions touched don’t matter once size is removed. Effort tracks how many places the change lands, not how much code is written.

How does the agent navigate scattered changes?
It searches more and starts editing before it has found everything.

  • More scattered → more searches and more files opened (ρ up to +0.89, surviving correction).
  • It finds files by grep, almost never by following calls or imports.
  • Scattered runs start editing earlier, having found 9% of the needed files vs 40% on localized runs, and discover the rest along the way.
  • More of their actions are reading (47% vs 32%) and fewer are git (4% vs 14%). Splitting by packages or dispersion instead shows no difference (table).

Can FeatureBench effort be read as search effort?
Only with care.

  • The agent reproduces code it was never shown (median 96% of reference lines verbatim; SWE-Pro 38%), so effort may reflect recall more than search.

Weaker results that don’t hold after correction: bottom of the page.

Read with care

  • All links are correlations, and the direction is open. More exploring can produce a more scattered diff, just as a scattered change can need more exploring.
  • Scattering is measured on the agent’s own diff, which can only include files it found.
  • Small samples: 21 + 61 runs, one seed each; the 61 SWE-Pro runs come from 10 repos (15 protonmail). 11 of them (batch 4) were picked because their reference patch changes ≥ 3 files.
  • Chart p-values are uncorrected; the appendix tables show corrected q.
How many correlations survive multiple-test correction? Benjamini–Hochberg q, applied separately to each table column (one benchmark × raw or size-adjusted).

Data. One agent (Claude Code 2.1.310, Opus 5.5), one run per task: 21 FeatureBench tasks across 6 Python repos, using a hand-written goal-only prompt, and 61 SWE-bench Pro V2 tasks across 10 repos in Python, Go and TypeScript, using the issue text. Each chart’s trend line is fitted within each benchmark, never across both.

Memorisation warning. On FeatureBench the agent’s diff reproduces a median 96% of reference lines verbatim, including 98% of comment lines, even though the prompt names no code. Those repos are very likely in training data, so effort there may reflect recall rather than navigation. SWE-Pro shows 38%. Read the two benchmarks separately.

Package dispersion (1 − HHI) has no unit; it runs from 0 to 1. HHI (Herfindahl–Hirschman Index) measures how concentrated the agent’s changed lines are across packages: take each package’s share of the changed lines, square each share and add them up. 1 − HHI flips it, so higher means more spread out.
How the changed lines are splitHHI1 − HHI
All in 1 package1.0² = 1.00

A package is the top two path components of a changed file.
How to read “FB ρ +0.60*”. Spearman rank correlation within one benchmark (−1 to +1; ≈ .3 weak, .5 moderate, ≥ .7 strong); * = permutation p < .05, uncorrected.
No star is not “no link”: FeatureBench has 21 runs, so ρ below about .45 often misses p < .05; SWE-Pro has 61, which detects about ρ ≥ .35. Correlation only, direction open.

Reading. After the size adjustment, 9 of 9 FeatureBench panels and 3 of 9 SWE-Pro panels still show p < .05. Within FeatureBench, more scattered diffs go with more tool calls, cost and searches than their size predicts (ρ about .5–.65). On SWE-Pro (61 runs) the raw links hold after correction (ρ about .3–.5) but shrink to ρ ≈ .1–.35 after the size adjustment and no longer survive correction (best q = .11): there, scattering adds little beyond size. This is associational: effort could scatter the change (more exploration, more files touched) as easily as the reverse.

Scattering vs navigation

Key findings (FeatureBench, 21 runs)

Only results that hold after correcting for multiple tests.

  • Scattered diffs go with more exploring. The more files the diff changes, the more the agent searched (ρ +.89) and the more files it opened (+.71). More packages and wider spread across packages also go with more files opened (+.54, +.56).
  • Focused diffs go with less exploring. The more of the diff sits in one file, the fewer searches (ρ −.82) and files opened (−.65), and the more needed files the agent had found before its first edit (+.63).
  • Wide diffs start editing earlier. Runs changing more files or functions had found fewer of the needed files before the first edit (ρ −.70, −.60).

Read with care

  • Scattering is measured on the agent’s own diff, and the agent can only change files it found, so navigation and scattering partly measure the same thing. Neither is shown to cause the other.
  • The findings above are FeatureBench only. On SWE-Pro (61 runs) the raw links also hold after correction: more files changed go with more files opened (ρ +.74) and more searches (+.48), and focused diffs with fewer (ρ −.68, −.43). Across low-recall runs of both benchmarks, more scattered diffs had more needed files first found by search (ρ ≈ +.4 to +.54, q < .05). See the appendix table.

Key findings (SWE-bench Pro, 61 runs)

Only results that hold after correcting for multiple tests.

  • Scattered diffs go with more exploring here too. The more files the diff changes, the more files the agent opened (ρ +.71) and the more it searched (+.47). More packages and wider spread also go with more files opened (+.58, +.58 in the appendix table, which leaves out 2 runs with no needed files).
  • Focused diffs go with less exploring. The more of the diff sits in one file, the fewer searches (ρ −.42) and files opened (−.68).
  • Split at the median: runs changing more than 1 file (28 of 61) opened a median 6 files vs 2 (r +.73), searched 7 vs 4 times (r +.42) and cost $0.38 vs $0.28 (r +.37). Runs touching more than one package opened 6 vs 3 (r +.66) and searched 8 vs 5 (r +.48). table

Different from FeatureBench

  • No “start editing earlier” effect. On FeatureBench, wide diffs had found fewer needed files before the first edit (ρ −.70). On SWE-Pro there is no such link (files changed ρ +.16, p = .22; median split 67% vs 33%, p = .21), possibly because the issue text often names the code to change. Functions touched even go the other way (ρ +.35, q = .02).
  • The action mix does not shift. On FeatureBench scattered runs read more and use git less. On SWE-Pro, no share of actions differs between scattered and localized runs (all q > .19).
  • Effects are smaller than on FeatureBench (median 9 tool calls per run, against 50), and correlations only.

Scattering vs technique

Probing does not rise with scattering: once size is removed, FeatureBench shows no link, and on SWE-Pro more scattered runs probe somewhat less (ρ ≈ −.28 to −.35, p < .05 but not surviving correction, q = .13). Codebook, validation and the full technique tables are in the appendix.

Task type vs scattering and effort

Each task was labelled from its prompt text only, before looking at any outcome (tasktype.csv, with a one-line reason per task). There are two labels. Nature has five groups: data/compute library core (10, all FeatureBench), plotting (4, FeatureBench), tool pipeline/integration such as CLIs, builders, clients and platform support (7 FeatureBench + 19 SWE-Pro), UI component/behaviour (12, SWE-Pro) and small fix/rename (30, SWE-Pro). Bundled marks a prompt that asks for several unrelated features at once (10 of the 21 FeatureBench tasks, no SWE-Pro task). Most groups exist in only one benchmark, so groups are compared within each benchmark (Kruskal–Wallis, permutation p): FeatureBench library/plotting/pipeline and SWE-Pro pipeline/UI/fix.

Findings. (1) Task nature goes with how a change is spread, not with how much effort it takes. On FeatureBench, package dispersion differs by nature (p = .01): library-core tasks stay inside one package (median dispersion .16), while plotting (.59) and pipeline tasks (.57) spread across packages. (2) On FeatureBench, effort (tool calls, cost) does not differ by nature, raw or size-adjusted. The closest is size-adjusted (p ≈ .07), where pipeline tasks run highest. On SWE-Pro it differs raw only, see (4). (3) Bundled multi-feature prompts lean bigger (median files 11.5 vs 6, tool calls 50 vs 28, cost $2.11 vs $1.28), but nothing is significant (p ≥ .39), and the gap disappears after the size adjustment. (4) On SWE-Pro (61 tasks: 30 fix, 19 pipeline, 12 UI), raw cost and tool calls differ by nature (cost p = .001, q = .005, median $0.23 fix, $0.33 pipeline, $0.40 UI; tool calls p = .012, q = .04, median 7.5, 9, 12.5; BH over the 6 SWE-Pro tests), but neither after the size adjustment (p = .08, .25): fixes are smaller changes. Labels are my reading of each prompt, so this is descriptive.

Scattering vs passing at the first attempt

Final diffs include what the agent changed after failure feedback, so here scattering is measured on the first-attempt diff (attempt1.diff.patch; for single-round runs the first attempt is the final diff). Only FeatureBench can be tested: all 61 SWE-Pro runs passed at the first attempt, so there is nothing to compare.

Finding. No scattering measure separates the 4 first-attempt failures from the 17 passes, raw or size-adjusted (all p > .4). The failures lean towards smaller first attempts: fewer lines and functions (r ≈ −.56, p ≈ .10). That looks more like under-doing the task than being lost in a scattered change. With 4 failures, only a very large effect could show up.

How to read r: rank-biserial correlation, from −1 to +1. Positive means failed runs tend to have higher values than passed runs. p = two-sided permutation test (5,000 shuffles of pass/fail labels). Size-adjusted = the measure’s residual after regressing it on log lines changed (FeatureBench only).

Scattering vs technique (SlopCodeBench codebook)

Every tool call is labelled with the same codebook used for SlopCodeBench (scbench/analysis/qual/techniques.py, hand-validated 57/60 on Python traces): read, edit tool, edit via script, probe (run code in the repo / scratch script in /tmp), run tests, static check. One call can carry several labels. For the Go/TS SWE-Pro tasks I added go test/jest/vitest, go run/node and go build/tsc/stylelint patterns. I hand-checked all 101 Go/TS Bash calls: 98/101 have the right label set; the 3 errors come from the unchanged base classifier (GOTS_VALIDATION.md).

Findings. (1) In FeatureBench almost every technique count rises with the number of files the agent changed; after the size adjustment the ones that stay at p < .05 are reads, script edits and test runs (ρ ≈ .5–.57), though none survives correction (q ≥ .08). (2) On SWE-Pro (61 runs) script edits and static checks (tsc, go build/vet) rise with scattering before size adjustment (ρ ≈ .32–.38), but none survive correction (q ≥ .056); after size adjustment only static checks vs packages / dispersion stay at p < .05 among them (ρ +.28, +.25, q = .13). The 12-run version of this page showed much stronger SWE-Pro technique links (ρ .7); they did not hold at 50 or 61. (3) Probing: in FeatureBench it rises with files only before size adjustment; in SWE-Pro, size-adjusted probing goes slightly down as scattering goes up (ρ ≈ −.28 to −.35, q = .13). (4) A focused change (most lines in one file) goes with fewer reads and script edits. 56 tests per benchmark (28 per column), with q per column — treat single cells as leads, not results; correlations only.

Benchmark vs benchmark

This comparison mixes prompt style, repository, language, size and memorisation, so it is kept for reference only. Shape variables in this appendix come from the reference patch.

FeatureBench, goal-onlySWE-bench Pro, issue text

How to compare the two benchmarks

Each benchmark is a group of cells (one run per task). For every variable we ask: if you pick one FeatureBench cell and one SWE-Pro cell at random, which is likely to be higher?

  • Cliff’s δ answers that directly. It runs from −1 (every SWE-Pro cell is higher) to +1 (every FeatureBench cell is higher), with 0 meaning no difference. |δ| below .15 is negligible, below .33 small, below .47 medium, and anything above is large. It uses ranks only, so a few extreme cells cannot drive it.
  • 95% CI comes from resampling cells (2,000 bootstraps). A CI that crosses 0 means the direction is not settled.
  • p is a permutation test (5,000 shuffles of the benchmark labels): how often a δ this large appears by chance. Pass rate uses Fisher’s exact test.
  • q is p after Benjamini-Hochberg correction within each variable group, because many variables are tested at once. Rows with q < .05 are shaded.
  • A difference here is associational. Benchmark, prompt style, repository, language and task size all change together.

Gold lines reproduced verbatim

The FeatureBench prompts name no code, yet the agent’s diff contains most reference lines character for character. That pattern is consistent with the reference being in training data. SWE-Pro, whose issue text does name code, shows much less overlap.

Gold lines reproduced verbatim, per cell

Each dot is one cell; the black tick is the median. Hover for task.

Comment-line matching

Comment wording is free, so a verbatim comment match is a sharper signal than matching code. Median match: 98% on FeatureBench against 0% on SWE-Pro. Only 40 of 61 SWE-Pro gold patches contain any comments; the 21 without any are left out.

Gold comment lines reproduced, per cell

Bar = share reproduced verbatim; “/n” = number of gold comment lines.

FeatureBenchSWE-bench Pro

Comment match tracks line recall closely (ρ ≈ .8). The effort gaps (tool calls, searches, cost) hold when it is used as the control instead (n = 61 runs with gold comments, p < .001).

Caveats

  1. Entangled factors. Benchmark, prompt style, repositories, language and task size change together.
  2. Verbatim recall is not proof of memorisation. It is used as a control, not a diagnosis.
  3. One seed per task. Run-to-run variance is unknown.
  4. SWE-Pro is spread over 10 repos (15 protonmail, 9 flipt, 7 each navidrome and vuls, 6 ansible, 5 qutebrowser, …); 12 runs come from earlier batches, 38 from batch 3 and 11 from batch 4. Batch 4 was selected for reference patches changing ≥ 3 files, so it is not a random draw. All use the issue text verbatim, except two prompts where one function or class name the tests don’t use was replaced.
  5. Small n. With 21 vs 61 cells, only |δ| above about .4 is reliably detectable. A non-significant row is not evidence of no difference.
  6. Function counts are parsed from patch text (def/class/func/function declarations and hunk headers), not from a parser.
  7. Regression checks on existing features are out of scope here.

Leads that do not survive correction

Each of these had uncorrected p < .05 but q ≥ .05 after Benjamini–Hochberg correction (task type: 6 Kruskal–Wallis tests per benchmark; p = .01 gives q = .06). They are directions to re-test with more runs, not results.

  1. Files vs effort on SWE-Pro. Size-adjusted, more files changed went with more searches and longer wall time (ρ +.34, p = .01, q = .11; wall time +.25, p = .06). Tool calls: ρ +.25, p = .06.
  2. Focus on SWE-Pro. Size-adjusted, more focused diffs went with fewer searches and shorter wall time (ρ −.32, −.31; p = .015, q = .11). Tool calls: ρ −.26, p = .05.
  3. Probing does not rise with scattering. On FeatureBench, the link between probes and files changed vanishes after the size adjustment. On SWE-Pro, more scattered runs probe slightly less than their size predicts (ρ ≈ −.28 to −.35). These come from 56 tests per benchmark, none surviving correction, so treat them as leads.
  4. Task type shapes the spread, not the effort. On FeatureBench, library-core tasks stay in one package (dispersion .16), while plotting and pipeline tasks spread across packages (.57–.59; p = .01). Tool calls and cost do not differ by task type on FeatureBench, and prompts that bundle several features are not significantly costlier. On SWE-Pro they differ raw (fixes are cheapest) but not after the size adjustment. Task type
